summary:
Police conduct is the clearest documented danger. In September 2017 national police in Baku detained at least 100 members of the LGBT community in raids conducted ostensibly against prostitution; beatings, forced medical examinations, interrogation and blackmail were documented, and a 2017 United States State Department report recorded threats of rape and the use of electric shocks. At least 60 people were imprisoned or fined, and the detentions formed part of a wave of arrests ahead of the Islamic Solidarity Games. Azerbaijan acknowledged the cases in 2019, and in April 2024 the European Court of Human Rights issued a ruling on the arrests and mistreatment.

In July 2023 officers raided a private birthday party in Baku, where queer guests were subjected to forced medical examinations, physical and sexual harassment, and threats of being outed.

A trans woman was murdered in Baku in March 2024 and the police investigation into the killing was inadequate. The response of the authorities is as significant as the violence itself: nothing in the record indicates that the state treats the killing of a trans woman as a matter requiring a serious investigation.

No law in Azerbaijan bans discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Trans people cannot change their gender on official documents, although they may change their name to match their gender identity; a shadow report to the CEDAW committee describes changing identity documents as impossible for trans women. Same-sex couples have no legal standing: marriage and civil unions are neither recognised nor performed, and same-sex couples may not adopt children. The age of consent is 16 for both heterosexual and homosexual sex. ILGA-Europe has ranked Azerbaijan last, 49 of 49, in Europe every year since 2015, citing a near total absence of legal protection.

Hostility is also carried by media and by families. State-affiliated Real TV aired discriminatory hate speech against LGBTI people after a Women's Day march in Baku demanding access to trans healthcare. An activist was told to remove a rainbow flag in a Baku cafe. In one documented case a family forcibly transported an 18-year-old woman to Baku after she came out.
tangentialFactors:
Hosting international events has repeatedly drawn criticism: critics have argued that Azerbaijan should not be allowed to host international events because of its discrimination against LGBTI people, a controversy that flared around the 2012 Eurovision song contest, and the September 2017 raids came immediately ahead of the Islamic Solidarity Games.

The media environment is documented as broadly hostile. QueeRadar monitoring found that 77% of 428 analysed media pieces were hateful or biased against LGBTIQ people, and media have been criticised for spreading fear and hate toward queer people through discriminatory language, with politicians and officials using that language to shape public perception. A 2017 United States State Department report recorded interference with expression, assembly and association through intimidation, incarceration on questionable charges and the blocking of websites.

Economic exclusion compounds the legal position. Discrimination against trans people has direct effects: rejection from jobs and housing, movement into black-market work and precarious housing. One profiled woman, Durdana, 29, was arrested, denied housing and employment, and left dependent on community support after her trans-friendly employer shut down.

International scrutiny exists but has not produced domestic change. A shadow report to the CEDAW committee at its 44th session documented state-approved ignorance, employment discrimination, militant homophobia and transphobia in official and private media, and forced marriages, and stated that the reporting organisation serves more than 200 LBT people. The April 2024 European Court of Human Rights ruling followed Azerbaijan's own 2019 acknowledgement of the 2017 cases.
localsOnly:
Conscription applies to able-bodied men aged 18 to 35. LGBTQIA+ enlistees can be declared unfit for service under Articles 18/b (personality disorders) and 17/b (reactive psychoses and neurotic disorders) of the Regulation on Military Medical Examinations, and queer conscripts often conceal their orientation to avoid dedovshchina hazing.

The constitution guarantees freedom of expression, and the Azerbaijan Press Council, founded in 2003, handles complaints under a Press Code of Conduct. LGBTQIA+ media nonetheless exists: gay.az, the first news website for LGBTQIA+ people, launched 25 May 2011, and Minority Magazine, founded in December 2015 and registered as an NGO from August 2017. A documentary about a trans man premiered in Baku on 25 November 2017 with Dutch embassy support and drew about 80 people.

Organised support is limited but present. The Gender Resource Center, established in 2020, is a queer-feminist platform created in response to the lack of safe space and resources for people of different genders and sexual orientations. Gender and Development, created in 2007, runs local projects in collaboration with the Ministry of Health. AZAD LGBT ran in-person programming in Baku, including LGBTQ movie nights attended by a local psychologist who joined post-film Q&As, and launched a website in 2015 providing free online LGBTQ education tools. Nafas LGBTI Azerbaijan Alliance regularly holds talks with the EU Delegation to Azerbaijan and other European embassies about the difficulties LGBTQ people face.

In April 2019 14-year-old Elina Hajiyeva of Baku attempted suicide after homophobic bullying at her school; the principal took no action, tried to attribute the attempt to family difficulties and did not call an ambulance, and she died in hospital two days later. The school director, deputy director and psychologist were dismissed, and on 24 October 2019 the Sabail District Court of Baku sentenced the principal to 2 years and 2.5 months of restricted liberty plus 18,500 AZN in compensation. The case sparked a nationwide social media campaign and a Ministry of Education anti-bullying action plan launched 13 May 2019 with a new hotline to improve school-family relations and protect students from abuse.
outOfScopeNotes:
Entry and visa rules for trans visitors are not sourced in this inventory, including whether gender markers on foreign passports are checked at the border or whether travellers face secondary screening that risks disclosure.

Whether the Azerbaijan Press Council has assessed complaints that state-controlled media used homosexuality to discredit government critics is not known.

Whether men who have sex with men are permitted to donate blood in practice is unknown; by law only people infected with HIV/AIDS are excluded.

The procedure, timeline and decision-making body for any form of legal gender recognition are unresolved beyond the statements that gender cannot be changed on official documents and that a name may be changed. No court route, medical requirement or waiting period is documented here.

Compliance with the April 2024 European Court of Human Rights ruling, including any compensation or reform ordered, is not stated in the sources.

No sourced information covers access to trans-specific healthcare, hormone therapy or surgical care, and whether the demands for trans healthcare raised at the Women's Day march were answered by the authorities is unresolved.
